modules.title: 10.1 General Properties of Metals and the Activity Series
modules.html:
About 80% of the known elements are metals. They occupy the left and centre of the periodic table and their atoms have few outer electrons which they readily lose to form cations.

Physical properties and their explanations

  • Metallic lustre — the sea of delocalised electrons reflects light.
  • Good conductors of heat and electricity — mobile electrons carry charge and energy.
  • Malleable and ductile — layers of positive ions slide past one another without breaking the metallic bond.
  • High density, high melting and boiling points — strong electrostatic attraction between cations and the electron sea. Exceptions: sodium and potassium are soft and float on water; mercury is liquid.
  • Sonorous — they ring when struck, hence bells and gongs.

Chemical properties

  1. With oxygen: basic oxides, \(4Na + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2O\); \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\). Oxides of Al, Zn, Pb and Sn are amphoteric.
  2. With water: K, Na and Ca react with cold water giving hydrogen; Mg, Zn and Fe react only with steam; Cu, Ag and Au do not react at all.
  3. With acids: metals above hydrogen in the activity series displace hydrogen from dilute acids: \(Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2\). Copper does not.

The activity (electrochemical) series

K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, [H], Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt — remembered by many Nigerian students as "King Nebuchadnezzar Called Many Angels Zealously Into Sacred Places, He Could Have Some Gold Plates."

The series predicts:

  • Displacement: a metal displaces any metal below it from solution, \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\) (blue solution fades, brown deposit forms).
  • Ease of extraction: very reactive metals (K to Al) must be extracted by electrolysis of the molten compound; those in the middle (Zn to Pb) by reduction with carbon; unreactive metals (Ag, Au, Pt) occur native.
  • Stability of compounds: the higher a metal is in the series, the more stable its oxide, hydroxide and trioxocarbonate are to heat.
  • Preferential discharge: in electrolysis, the ion of the metal lower in the series is discharged first at the cathode.

Occurrence and terminology

A mineral is any naturally occurring compound of a metal; an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably. Common Nigerian ores include cassiterite \(SnO_2\) (Jos Plateau), haematite \(Fe_2O_3\) (Itakpe), and columbite. Extraction has three stages: concentration (froth flotation, magnetic separation, washing), reduction (smelting or electrolysis) and refining (usually electrolytic).
examples: Explain why potassium cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon.
Predict what happens when an iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulphate solution.

modules.title: 10.2 Extraction of Aluminium, Iron, Copper and Tin; Alloys
modules.html:
Aluminium — the Hall-Héroult process

Ore: bauxite, \(Al_2O_3\!\cdot\!2H_2O\). It is purified by the Bayer process: the amphoteric alumina dissolves in hot concentrated \(NaOH\) while iron(III) oxide impurity does not, and the filtrate is later precipitated and calcined to pure \(Al_2O_3\).

Electrolysis: pure alumina melts at over \(2000^{\circ}C\), so it is dissolved in molten cryolite \(Na_3AlF_6\), which lowers the working temperature to about \(950^{\circ}C\) and increases conductivity. Graphite anodes dip into a steel tank lined with graphite (the cathode).

Cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\)    Anode: \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\)

The oxygen attacks the hot graphite anodes, which burn away and must be replaced regularly — a major running cost, along with the enormous electricity demand (hence smelters are built near hydroelectric power).

Properties and uses: aluminium is light, resistant to corrosion because of a self-repairing oxide film (thickened deliberately by anodising), and a good conductor. It is used in aircraft bodies, overhead cables with a steel core, cooking utensils, foil and, as thermite (\(2Al + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2Fe\)), for welding rails.

Iron — the blast furnace

Ores: haematite \(Fe_2O_3\), magnetite \(Fe_3O_4\), siderite \(FeCO_3\), iron pyrites \(FeS_2\). The charge is ore, coke and limestone; hot air is blasted in at the base.

  1. \(C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2\) (exothermic, raises temperature to about \(1900^{\circ}C\))
  2. \(CO_2 + C \rightarrow 2CO\) (the reducing agent)
  3. \(Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2\)
  4. \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\); \(CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3\) (slag, which floats on the molten iron and is tapped separately for road-making and cement)

The product, pig iron, contains about 4% carbon and is brittle. Removing carbon in the basic-oxygen furnace gives steel; adding chromium and nickel gives stainless steel. Wrought iron is the purest commercial form.

Rusting requires both oxygen and water; salt accelerates it. Prevention: painting, greasing, galvanising (zinc coating that also gives sacrificial protection), tin-plating, electroplating, alloying and cathodic protection with magnesium blocks.

Copper and tin

Copper is roasted from copper pyrites \(CuFeS_2\), converted to blister copper and then refined electrolytically: impure copper is the anode, pure copper the cathode and \(CuSO_4\) solution the electrolyte; the anode mud yields silver and gold as valuable by-products. Copper is used in electrical wiring, coins and alloys.

Tin comes from cassiterite \(SnO_2\), reduced with carbon: \(SnO_2 + 2C \rightarrow Sn + 2CO\). It is used for tin-plating steel cans and in the alloys solder, bronze and pewter.

Alloys

AlloyCompositionUse
BrassCu + ZnOrnaments, taps, musical instruments
BronzeCu + SnStatues, coins, bearings
SteelFe + CConstruction, tools
Stainless steelFe + Cr + NiCutlery, sinks, surgical tools
DuraluminAl + Cu + Mg + MnAircraft parts
SolderPb + SnJoining electrical wires

Alloys are made to increase hardness and strength, improve corrosion resistance, lower melting point (solder) or improve appearance.
examples: State the role of cryolite and of limestone in the two extraction processes.
Write the three main reduction equations in the blast furnace.

modules.title: 10.3 Compounds of Metals and Qualitative Analysis
modules.html:
Beyond extraction, the examination expects a working knowledge of the chemistry of the common metal compounds and of the qualitative-analysis reactions used to identify their ions.

Sodium and its compounds

Sodium is extracted by the Downs process, the electrolysis of molten \(NaCl\) with \(CaCl_2\) added to lower the melting point. It is stored under kerosene because it reacts violently with air and water. Key compounds: \(NaOH\) (caustic soda, from brine electrolysis, used in soap and paper), \(Na_2CO_3\) (Solvay process, used in glass and water softening), \(NaHCO_3\) (baking) and \(NaCl\).

Calcium and its compounds

\(CaCO_3\) (limestone, marble, chalk) heated in a lime kiln gives quicklime: \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\). Quicklime slaked with water gives slaked lime, \(CaO + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2\), whose solution is lime water. Calcium compounds are used in cement (limestone + clay), mortar, plaster of Paris \(CaSO_4\!\cdot\!\tfrac{1}{2}H_2O\), and in neutralising acidic soils.

Zinc, lead and their amphoteric behaviour

\(ZnO\), \(PbO\), \(Al_2O_3\) and \(Sn O\) react with both acids and alkalis:

\(ZnO + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_2 + H_2O\) and \(ZnO + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2ZnO_2 + H_2O\).

Lead compounds show striking colours: \(PbI_2\) is yellow, \(PbCrO_4\) is yellow, \(PbS\) is black; lead(II) oxide is yellow when hot and turns red on cooling as \(Pb_3O_4\) forms on strong heating in air.

Transition metals

The d-block metals (Fe, Cu, Zn, Cr, Mn, Ni) are characterised by:

  • Variable oxidation states: \(Fe^{2+}/Fe^{3+}\), \(Cu^{+}/Cu^{2+}\), \(Mn^{2+}\) to \(Mn^{7+}\).
  • Coloured ions: \(Fe^{2+}\) pale green, \(Fe^{3+}\) yellow-brown, \(Cu^{2+}\) blue, \(MnO_4^{-}\) purple, \(Cr_2O_7^{2-}\) orange.
  • Catalytic activity: Fe in Haber, \(V_2O_5\) in Contact, Ni in hydrogenation, \(MnO_2\) in the decomposition of \(H_2O_2\).
  • Complex-ion formation: \(Cu(NH_3)_4^{2+}\), \(Fe(CN)_6^{4-}\).
  • Paramagnetism from unpaired d-electrons.

Strictly, zinc is not a true transition metal because its \(3d\) sub-shell is full in both the atom and the \(Zn^{2+}\) ion.

Give the flame colours of sodium, potassium, calcium and copper.

modules.title: 10.4 Corrosion, Faraday Calculations and Applications
modules.html:
Metal extraction questions almost always mix a description with a Faraday or a stoichiometric calculation. Master the three templates below and you can answer nearly any variant.

Template 1 — electrolysis and Faraday's laws

\(Q = It\) and \(1\ F = 96500\ C\,mol^{-1}\) of electrons. Mass \(m = \dfrac{ItM}{nF}\), where \(n\) is the charge on the ion.

Example: Calculate the mass of aluminium deposited when a current of 40 A flows for 5 hours through molten alumina. (\(Al = 27\)).

\(Q = 40 \times (5\times3600) = 720\,000\ C\). Moles of electrons \(= 720000/96500 = 7.461\ mol\).

\(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\), so \(n(Al) = 7.461/3 = 2.487\ mol\); \(m = 2.487\times27 = \mathbf{67.2\ g}\).

Template 2 — ore to metal

Example: What mass of iron is obtained from 1 tonne of haematite that is 80% \(Fe_2O_3\)? (\(Fe=56, O=16\)).

Mass of \(Fe_2O_3 = 0.80 \times 1000\ kg = 800\ kg\). \(M(Fe_2O_3) = 160\), and 160 kg contains \(112\ kg\) of iron.

Mass of iron \(= 800 \times \dfrac{112}{160} = \mathbf{560\ kg}\).

Template 3 — percentage composition

Example: Find the percentage by mass of copper in \(CuSO_4\!\cdot\!5H_2O\). (\(Cu=64, S=32, O=16, H=1\)).

\(M = 64 + 32 + 64 + 90 = 250\). Percentage \(= (64/250)\times100 = \mathbf{25.6\%}\).

Corrosion: a closer look

Rusting is an electrochemical process. At the anodic region \(Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-\); at the cathodic region \(O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-\). The \(Fe(OH)_2\) formed is oxidised further to hydrated iron(III) oxide, \(Fe_2O_3\!\cdot\!xH_2O\), which is rust. Because rust flakes off, it does not protect the metal beneath — unlike aluminium oxide, which does.

  • Galvanising: zinc corrodes preferentially because it is higher in the activity series, so protection continues even if the coating is scratched.
  • Tin-plating: tin is below iron, so a scratch actually accelerates rusting — a favourite examination contrast with galvanising.
  • Cathodic protection: magnesium or zinc blocks bolted to ships' hulls and buried pipelines act as sacrificial anodes.

Economic and environmental notes

Extraction is energy-intensive; recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of the energy of primary production. Mining causes land degradation and acid-mine drainage, while smelters emit \(SO_2\) from sulphide ores — a cause of acid rain. Nigeria's Ajaokuta steel complex and the Jos tin fields are the standard local examples to cite in essay answers.
examples: Calculate the mass of copper deposited by 2 A flowing for 30 minutes.
Explain why galvanising protects iron but tin-plating can worsen rusting.

quiz.q: Metals are good conductors of electricity because they have
quiz.solution: A sea of mobile electrons carries the current.

quiz.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
quiz.solution: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at 25 C.

quiz.q: Metals are malleable because
options: layers of cations can slide without breaking the metallic bond
quiz.solution: The delocalised electrons keep the layers bonded as they slide.

quiz.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.solution: Zinc oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis.

quiz.q: Which metal does NOT liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
quiz.solution: Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series.

quiz.q: The correct order of decreasing reactivity is
quiz.solution: Potassium and calcium are far above zinc, which is above copper.

quiz.q: Metals from potassium to aluminium are extracted by
quiz.solution: They are too reactive to be reduced by carbon.

quiz.q: An ore is
options: a mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted
a pure metal found in nature
quiz.solution: Profitability distinguishes an ore from a mineral.

quiz.q: The chief ore of aluminium is
quiz.solution: Bauxite is hydrated aluminium oxide.

quiz.q: Cryolite is added in aluminium extraction to
options: lower the melting point of alumina and improve conductivity
quiz.solution: It lets electrolysis run near 950 C instead of over 2000 C.

quiz.q: The anodes in the aluminium cell burn away because
options: oxygen liberated attacks the hot graphite
quiz.solution: Oxygen oxidises the carbon anodes to CO2.

quiz.q: At the cathode in aluminium extraction
quiz.solution: Reduction always occurs at the cathode.

quiz.q: Aluminium resists corrosion because
options: a tough adherent oxide layer forms
quiz.solution: The oxide film is impervious and self-repairing.

quiz.q: Thickening the oxide layer on aluminium electrolytically is called
quiz.solution: Anodising also allows dyeing of the surface.

quiz.q: The chief ore of iron used in the blast furnace is
quiz.solution: Haematite, Fe2O3, is the commonest iron ore.

quiz.q: In the blast furnace limestone
quiz.solution: CaO from limestone combines with SiO2 to form calcium trioxosilicate(IV).

quiz.q: The main reducing agent in the blast furnace is
quiz.solution: CO formed from CO2 and coke reduces the ore.

quiz.q: Pig iron is brittle because it contains about
quiz.solution: About four percent carbon makes cast iron hard but brittle.

quiz.q: Stainless steel contains iron with
quiz.solution: Chromium and nickel confer corrosion resistance.

quiz.q: The purest commercial form of iron is
quiz.solution: Wrought iron contains very little carbon.

quiz.q: Rusting requires
quiz.solution: Both are essential; salt merely accelerates the process.

quiz.q: Galvanising protects iron even when scratched because zinc is
options: below iron in the activity series
above iron in the activity series
quiz.solution: Zinc corrodes preferentially, giving sacrificial protection.

quiz.q: A scratch in tin-plated steel accelerates rusting because tin is
options: above iron in the activity series
below iron in the activity series
quiz.solution: Iron becomes the anode of the tin-iron cell.

quiz.q: Copper is refined by
options: electrolysis with impure copper as anode
quiz.solution: Pure copper deposits on the cathode; anode mud yields silver and gold.

quiz.q: The ore of tin is
quiz.solution: Cassiterite is tin(IV) oxide, mined on the Jos Plateau.

quiz.q: Brass is an alloy of
quiz.solution: Brass is copper with zinc.

quiz.q: Bronze is an alloy of
quiz.solution: Bronze is copper with tin.

quiz.q: Solder is used in electrical work because it
quiz.solution: The lead-tin alloy melts at a conveniently low temperature.

quiz.q: Duralumin is used in aircraft because it is
quiz.solution: An aluminium alloy combines low density with strength.

quiz.q: Sodium is extracted by the
quiz.solution: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride gives sodium and chlorine.

quiz.q: Sodium is stored under kerosene because it
options: reacts vigorously with air and water
quiz.solution: Kerosene keeps out air and moisture.

quiz.q: Heating limestone strongly produces
quiz.solution: CaCO3 gives CaO and CO2 in the lime kiln.

quiz.q: Slaked lime is
quiz.solution: Adding water to quicklime produces calcium hydroxide.

quiz.q: Plaster of Paris is
quiz.solution: The hemihydrate sets hard when mixed with water.

quiz.q: Which ion gives a reddish-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide?
quiz.solution: Iron(III) hydroxide is reddish-brown and insoluble in excess.

quiz.q: A white precipitate soluble in both excess NaOH and excess ammonia indicates
quiz.solution: Only zinc hydroxide dissolves in both reagents.

quiz.q: Aluminium ion with excess sodium hydroxide gives
quiz.solution: Amphoteric Al(OH)3 dissolves to form the aluminate.

quiz.q: A pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia to a deep blue solution indicates
quiz.solution: The tetraamminecopper(II) ion is deep blue.

quiz.q: The flame colour of calcium is
quiz.solution: Calcium gives a brick-red flame.

quiz.q: The flame colour of potassium is
quiz.solution: Potassium gives a lilac flame, best seen through cobalt-blue glass.

quiz.q: Transition metals are good catalysts partly because they
quiz.solution: Variable oxidation states allow easy electron transfer.

quiz.q: Zinc is not regarded as a true transition metal because
options: its d sub-shell is completely filled
quiz.solution: Neither Zn nor Zn2+ has a partly filled d sub-shell.

quiz.q: The colour of the heptaoxodichromate(VI) ion is
quiz.solution: Cr2O7 2- is orange and is reduced to green Cr3+.

quiz.q: One faraday is equal to
quiz.solution: One faraday is the charge on one mole of electrons.

quiz.q: The mass of aluminium deposited by 3 faradays is (Al = 27)
quiz.solution: Al3+ needs 3 F per mole, so 3 F gives 1 mol = 27 g.

quiz.q: A current of 40 A for 5 hours deposits how much aluminium? (Al=27)
quiz.solution: Q = 720000 C; 7.46 mol electrons / 3 = 2.49 mol Al.

quiz.q: 1 tonne of ore containing 80% Fe2O3 yields how much iron? (Fe=56, O=16)
quiz.solution: 800 kg of Fe2O3 contains 800 x 112/160 = 560 kg iron.

quiz.q: The percentage of copper in CuSO4.5H2O (M = 250, Cu = 64) is
Recycling aluminium is encouraged mainly because it
options: saves about 95% of the energy of primary extraction
quiz.solution: Remelting scrap avoids the huge electrolysis energy cost.

quiz.q: Which is used as a sacrificial anode on ships' hulls?
quiz.solution: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead.
